text: A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium when the forward and the reverse reaction go at the same rate: it doesn't stop, because both reactions keep going. Le Châtelier's principle says that if I disturb an equilibrium, the system shifts to counteract the disturbance: for example, if I add N2 the equilibrium shifts towards NH3 to consume part of it. The catalyst also shifts the equilibrium towards the products.

At equilibrium the reaction stops and nothing happens any more. The catalyst does not shift the equilibrium, because it speeds up the forward and the reverse reaction equally: equilibrium is just reached sooner.
Le Châtelier. Dynamic equilibrium. Catalyst. Equilibrium constant Kc. Temperature.

The equilibrium constant Kc depends only on temperature, so if I add a reactant the concentrations change but Kc stays the same. The reaction quotient Q has the same form as Kc: if Q is smaller than K the reaction goes towards the products.

If the reaction is exothermic and I raise the temperature, K decreases because heat behaves like a product and the equilibrium shifts towards the reactants. Le Châtelier's principle predicts it: the system counteracts the temperature increase.
The catalyst is there to get more product at equilibrium, that's why iron is used in Haber-Bosch. Le Châtelier says the equilibrium shifts.

To me equilibrium is like an escalator going up and one going down at the same speed: people are always moving, but there are always lots of them on each floor. In other words the reactions keep going but the concentrations stay constant.
Raising the temperature always increases K, for every reaction. The reaction quotient is something you calculate.
